sweep_summary: Niuean (niue1239) is in the catalog as kind=weight (penultimate mora; final long vowel/diphthong stressed) on Brown & Tukuitonga 2018 JIPA, backed by held copies of Rolle & Starks 2014 and Rolle 2009, plus Zuraw 2018 fetched sources in the earlier audit. The title sweep produced exactly one item, Clemens 2019 (Syntax 22(4):337-377, doi:10.1111/synt.12170, already in the per-language bibliography). The Wiley copy is closed (Unpaywall/Semantic Scholar: CLOSED; OpenAlex: no record), but the author's LingBuzz 004182 preprint ('to appear in Syntax', Sept 2018) is open; The paper is about phrasal prosody and syntax (VSO vs VOS pseudo-noun incorporation, H*L- tunes per phi-phrase), not word stress; its single stress sentence (sec. 2.2, preprint p. 8) says stress falls on the penultimate syllable of most words and on the final syllable when it ends in a long vowel or diphthong, citing Rolle & Starks 2014. This confirms the catalog coding and adds nothing first-hand; it does not supersede Brown & Tukuitonga 2018. Nothing remains to acquire from this sweep (priority none). The only unheld carried primary remains Sperlich 1997:10 (print-only dictionary intro), already on the wishlist at low priority.

new_statements.reading: Penultimate-syllable stress by default; a word-final long vowel or diphthong (a heavy final syllable) takes the stress instead. That is the same right-edge, weight-sensitive (equivalently penultimate-mora) pattern the catalog codes as kind=weight from Brown & Tukuitonga 2018. It is the only stress statement in the paper, and it is a carrier citing Rolle & Starks 2014 rather than a first-hand description, although Clemens' own pitch-track data (H* anchored to those syllables) are consistent with it.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the held open-access publisher PDF text layer at the stated pages (121-122), and both secondary quotations (Rolle & Starks 2014 pp.276-278; Rolle 2009 TWPL 31 pp.5-6) are verbatim in held files. Deciding source is a 2018 JIPA Illustration, the standard modern phonetic description for the language, supported by a 2014 Oceanic Linguistics phonology article with measurements and a 2014 Harvard prosody dissertation (both held, both agreeing: penultimate mora = penult syllable by default, final long vowel/diphthong stressed, breaking of penultimate VV before final CV). Glottolog's higher-ranked 'grammars' (Seiter 1980, Massam 2020) are syntax monographs; no reference grammar with a phonology chapter exists that would outrank the JIPA piece. sources.citation: Clemens, Lauren. 2019. Prosodic noun incorporation: The relationship between prosody and argument structure in Niuean. Syntax 22(4): 337-377. doi:10.1111/synt.12170. (Glottolog 606337, hhtype grammar_sketch; already_listed.) Held copy: LingBuzz 004182 author preprint, September 2018, 'to appear in Syntax', 56 pp.
sources.quote: Niuean clauses are produced with a series of H*L- tunes corresponding to phonological phrases (ϕ-phrases). The H* for each ϕ-phrase is located on the rightmost prosodic word (PWd) of the phrase. H* tones are anchored to stressed syllables; stress is located on the penultimate syllable of most words and the final syllable of words that end with a long vowel or a diphthong (Rolle and Starks 2014). Thus, a H* tone can serve as a diagnostic for the right edge of Niuean ϕ-phrases.
sources.locator: Preprint sec. 2.2 'The Prosody of Niuean PNI', preprint p. 8 (text file lines 328-333); footnote 7 on the same page. Published pagination (Syntax 22(4):337-377) not verified because the Wiley copy is closed.
sources.note: The paper is a syntax-prosody interface study of VSO vs VOS (pseudo-noun-incorporation) word order and phonological phrasing (H*L- tunes per phi-phrase, pitch tracks from the author's own recordings). Word stress is treated in one sentence, and that sentence is attributed to Rolle & Starks 2014, not first-hand: default penultimate-syllable stress, final stress when the last syllable has a long vowel or diphthong. sources.quote: 'NIUEAN. In Niuean (Sperlich 1997), which is closely related to Tongan, monomorphemes can contain breaking, as illustrated ... ha(áu) 'your', ha(áku) 'mine', ha(ána) 'their', mo(óli) 'true', ma(áma) 'bright', fo(óu) 'new'' ; ''rearticulation' tends to mean 'occurrence of pitch rise or other correlates of stress on second half of long vowel', and this does not apply to [fáa]'. Niuean classed as a breaking (penultimate-mora, word-final bimoraic trochee) system like Tongan.
